Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retired
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
At sixty-eight, Mary Johnson can still recall every detail of the phone call two years ago—the way the kitchen clock read 11:17, the clatter of the receiver as she dropped it, the strange stillness of the house afterward. Her son David had been killed instantly when his car drifted off a rain-slicked highway. He was thirty-four. She had spoken to him that evening, had even mentioned the worsening weather, but she had not insisted he stay home. That single omission became a splinter she could not remove. In the weeks that followed, she told herself she should have done more, should have been firmer, should have protected him. The thought lodged itself in her chest and would not leave.

At first, Mary tried to navigate the grief as everyone expected. She attended the service, accepted casseroles, and listened to condolences. But she soon found she could not bear the weight of other people’s sympathy. When her bridge club called, she let the machine pick up. When her neighbor came by with a pot of soup, Mary stood behind the door until she heard her footsteps recede. She started to feel as though she no longer belonged anywhere—not among her friends, not in her own skin. The women she had laughed with for decades now seemed to inhabit a different world, one where the worst thing was still a possibility and not a certainty. She began to believe she was set apart, marked by something invisible that others could sense. In her late sixties, a time when many of her peers were enjoying retirement cruises and grandchildren, she found herself shrinking from every invitation, certain she would only cast a pall over any gathering.

To stop the spiraling thoughts, Mary kept moving. She woke before dawn and scrubbed the bathrooms, reorganized the pantry, weeded the garden until her hands ached. She volunteered for every odd job at the church that required no conversation: folding bulletins, polishing brass. Being busy, she told herself, was the only way to outrun the moment when the silence would press in. But her body never seemed to get the message. Her shoulders stayed hunched, her jaw tight. Even when she sat down to watch television with her husband, Robert, she felt poised for disaster—her muscles tensed, her ears straining for an ambulance siren or a phone that might ring again. She could not relax, not even in the living room she had decorated herself.

The negative emotions came in waves, often without warning. Fear would grip her when she saw a young man in a baseball cap walking toward her. Horror surfaced when a car braked sharply outside. Anger rose at the driver who had been in the other lane, at the road, at the rain, at herself—then guilt would wash over her for being angry, and shame for feeling anything at all. She sometimes wept in the laundry room, pressing a towel against her mouth so Robert would not hear. She felt she had no right to fall apart when she was the one who should have kept David safe. Even her age seemed to mock her: she had lived long enough to see her son buried, yet felt utterly helpless, a mother who had failed at the one job that mattered most.

Months passed, then a year. Mary’s avoidance became routine. She stopped going to the grocery store during peak hours to avoid running into acquaintances. She declined all invitations, eventually stopped returning calls. Her only contact was Robert, and even with him she felt a growing distance. He would try to hold her hand, and she would feel her body stiffen, unable to receive comfort. They ate dinner in near silence. She knew he was worried, but she could not explain what she herself hardly understood: that being near him felt like failing all over again, as if her inability to protect David had stained her, made her unfit for ordinary closeness.

What finally brought Mary to a therapist’s office was not a sudden decision but a slow erosion. Robert had gently said he did not know how to help her anymore. She had looked at his tired face, at the years they had shared, and realized she was making him carry something alone. That night, she lay awake, her legs restless, her mind replaying the phone call. She thought about her friends, her church, her son—all gone from her life. At sixty-eight, she understood she was living in a kind of exile she had built herself, though she could not see how to leave it. In the therapist’s waiting room, she sat with her hands folded tightly, afraid that no words could reach her and terrified that if they did, the fragile structure she had built around her grief might collapse entirely.
